pages.title: What is Data Science & Datification?
pages.content_html:
1.1 What is Data Science?

You have already experienced data science in several forms: when searching the web, asking mobile phones for directions, or receiving personalized recommendations. Data science is commonly defined as a methodology by which actionable insights can be inferred from data.

Data science builds upon centuries of mathematical and statistical foundations, standing on the shoulders of eighteenth-century giants such as Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749-1827) and Thomas Bayes (1701-1761), combined with modern computational machine learning.

The Concept of Datification

The novelty of modern data science is rooted in datification: the process of rendering into data aspects of the world that have never been quantified before. At the personal level, our web browsing, books read, music listened to, driving behavior, and social interactions are datified. At the enterprise level, servers capture web activity logs, sensor signals, machine telemetry, and customer communications for predictive analysis.

Four Core Strategies to Explore Data

  1. Probing Reality: Gathering data via passive or active methods (e.g. A/B testing in web platforms to determine optimal UX choices).
  2. Pattern Discovery: Dividing complex problems to discover useful patterns, natural clusters, and consumer behavioral profiles.
  3. Predicting Future Events: Building robust mathematical models to forecast future samples and take proactive decisions.
  4. Understanding People & the World: Leveraging deep learning for natural language processing, computer vision, and cognitive systems.

pages.title: Toolboxes for Data Scientists & Why Python?
pages.content_html:
1.2 Toolboxes for Data Scientists

Choosing the right tools allows data scientists to focus directly on data analysis rather than boilerplate code. In modern data science, Python has emerged as the universal language of choice.

ParadigmLanguagesCharacteristics
High-Performance / ProductionC, C++, JavaCompiled, high execution speed, static typing, verbose syntax.
Scripting / PrototypingRuby, Perl, PythonInterpreted, dynamic typing, concise syntax, fast experimentation.

Why Python for Data Science?

  • Simplicity: Clean, highly readable syntax without mandatory semicolon delimiters or boilerplates.
  • Multi-Paradigm: Supports Object-Oriented, Functional, and Procedural programming paradigms natively.
  • Rich Scientific Ecosystem:
    • NumPy: Multi-dimensional array structures (ndarray), vectorization, and linear algebra routines.
    • SciPy: Scientific algorithms for optimization, signal processing, and integration.
    • Pandas: High-performance DataFrame structures with integrated indexing for structured tabular data.
    • Scikit-Learn: Machine learning algorithms for classification, regression, clustering, and model selection.
    • Matplotlib & Seaborn: Publication-quality 2D charting, statistical distributions, and heatmaps.

Interactive Environment: Jupyter Notebooks

Jupyter Notebook provides a web-based interactive development environment (WIDE) running on http://localhost:8888. It allows data scientists to weave together executable Python code cells, markdown documentation, mathematical formulas, and inline plots.

pages.title: Pandas DataFrame Structure & Reading Data
pages.content_html:
1.3 The DataFrame Data Structure

The key data structure in Pandas is the DataFrame: a two-dimensional tabular data structure with labeled axes (rows as indexes, and columns as Series). It functions like an ultra-fast in-memory spreadsheet.

Creating a DataFrame from Python Dictionaries

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

data = {
    'year': [2010, 2011, 2012, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2010, 2011, 2012],
    'team': ['FCBarcelona', 'FCBarcelona', 'FCBarcelona', 
             'RMadrid', 'RMadrid', 'RMadrid', 
             'ValenciaCF', 'ValenciaCF', 'ValenciaCF'],
    'wins': [30, 28, 32, 29, 32, 26, 21, 17, 19],
    'draws': [6, 7, 4, 5, 4, 7, 8, 10, 8],
    'losses': [2, 3, 2, 4, 2, 5, 9, 11, 11]
}
football = pd.DataFrame(data, columns=['year', 'team', 'wins', 'draws', 'losses'])
print(football.head())

Reading Real-World Tabular Datasets

Most real-world data is distributed in Comma-Separated Values (CSV) format. Pandas provides the high-performance read_csv() method:

# Reading Eurostat Educational Indicators dataset
edu = pd.read_csv('educ_figdp_1_Data.csv',
                  na_values=':',
                  usecols=['TIME', 'GEO', 'Value'])

# Inspecting the data structure
print("Dimensions:", edu.shape)      # Output: 384 rows x 3 columns
print(edu.head())                    # First 5 rows
print(edu.describe())                # Descriptive statistical summary

pages.title: Selecting, Slicing & Boolean Filtering
pages.content_html:
1.4 Selecting, Slicing & Filtering Data

Pandas provides expressive operators to slice and filter data subsets based on position, column name, or conditional logic.

Selecting Columns & Slicing Rows

# 1. Select a single column (returns a Series)
values_series = edu['Value']

# 2. Slice rows by position index (10th to 13th rows)
subset_rows = edu[10:14]

# 3. Label-based selection using .loc / .iloc
subset_grid = edu.loc[90:94, ['TIME', 'GEO']]

Boolean Filtering (Masking)

Filtering rows based on conditional expressions creates a Boolean mask (True/False array) that subsets the data:

# Filter countries spending more than 6.5% on education
high_spending = edu[edu['Value'] > 6.5].tail()
print(high_spending)
# Output: Belgium, Cyprus, Malta, Finland (2002-2011)

Handling Missing Values (NaN)

In real datasets, missing entries are represented as NaN (Not a Number). In Python, NaN != NaN, so the isnull() function must be used:

# Filter rows containing missing values
missing_records = edu[edu['Value'].isnull()].head()

# Option A: Drop records with missing values
clean_edu = edu.dropna(how='any', subset=['Value'])

# Option B: Impute missing values with a constant or mean
filled_edu = edu.fillna(value={'Value': 0})

pages.title: Aggregations, Groupby, Pivoting & Ranking
pages.content_html:
1.5 Data Manipulation & Transformation

Modern analytics requires transforming raw tabular structures into aggregated and reshaped formats for downstream modeling.

Applying Custom & Lambda-Functions

# Normalizing educational expenditure by dividing by column maximum
edu['ValueNorm'] = edu['Value'] / edu['Value'].max()

# Applying custom mathematical functions via lambda
edu['Value_Squared'] = edu['Value'].apply(lambda d: d ** 2)

# Dropping temporary columns (inplace=True mutates original DataFrame)
edu.drop('Value_Squared', axis=1, inplace=True)

Grouping Data (Groupby)

# Compute mean educational expenditure per country across all years
country_means = edu[['GEO', 'Value']].groupby('GEO').mean()
print(country_means.head())

Pivoting Tabular Structures

Transforming rows into columns creates a spreadsheet-style pivot matrix:

# Pivot data: Countries as Index, Years as Columns
filtered_data = edu[edu['TIME'] > 2005]
pivedu = pd.pivot_table(filtered_data, values='Value', index=['GEO'], columns=['TIME'])
print(pivedu.head())

Ranking Data

# Rank countries descending by educational funding
pivedu_ranked = pivedu.rank(ascending=False, method='first')

# Sum all years and find top 5 countries
top_5 = pivedu.sum(axis=1).rank(ascending=False, method='dense').sort_values().head(5)
# Output: Denmark, Cyprus, Finland, Malta, Belgium

pages.title: Populations, Samples & Data Preparation
pages.content_html:
2.1 Populations, Samples & Data Preparation

Statistics is built upon two core concepts:

  • Population: The complete collection of objects, items, or individuals about which information is sought.
  • Sample: A carefully observed representative subset drawn from the population.

The 4-Step Data Preparation Pipeline

1 Obtaining Data

Acquiring raw data from files, databases, web scraping, or live sensor feeds.

2 Parsing Data

Decoding raw text formats (CSV, JSON, XML, fixed-width tables) into memory structures.

3 Cleaning Data

Detecting anomalies, handling non-responses, eliminating corrupted records.

4 Building Data Structures

Representing samples in memory-efficient DataFrames or out-of-memory key-value databases.

Case Study: The Adult Census Dataset

The UCI Adult dataset comprises 32,561 records across 15 attributes (age, education, occupation, sex, hours per week, capital gain, income). We can explore demographic hypotheses such as comparing earnings ratios across age and gender segments.

pages.title: Measures of Central Tendency & Dispersion
pages.content_html:
2.2 Central Tendency & Dispersion

Summarizing quantitative variables requires numerical descriptors that capture both the center and the spread of data.

Sample Mean & Variance

Given a sample of n observations x1, x2, ..., xn, the Sample Mean μ is:

μ = (1 / n) Σ xi

The Sample Variance σ² measures the dispersion of values around the mean:

σ² = (1 / n) Σ (xi - μ)²

The Standard Deviation σ = √(σ²) is preferred in practice because it retains the original physical units of the measurement (e.g., years, dollars, kilograms).

The Sample Median & Robustness to Outliers

While the mean is sensitive to extreme values, the Sample Median μ1/2 is an order statistic that identifies the exact middle element when sorted.

The Impact of Outliers

In a dataset of weekly work hours [40, 42, 38, 45, 1000], the sample mean surges from 41 to 233 hours due to a single data entry mistake! However, the sample median remains robust at 42 hours, demonstrating why the median is the preferred central descriptor in the presence of noise.

pages.title: Quantiles, Percentiles & Distributions
pages.content_html:
2.3 Quantiles, Percentiles & Distributions

To examine the complete profile of a variable, data is partitioned into percentiles and visualized through distribution curves.

The 5-Number Summary & IQR

The sample is divided into quartiles:

  • Q1 (25th Percentile): First quartile (25% of observations fall below this value).
  • Q2 (50th Percentile): Median of the dataset.
  • Q3 (75th Percentile): Third quartile (75% of observations fall below this value).
  • Interquartile Range (IQR): IQR = Q3 - Q1, capturing the middle 50% of the distribution.

Histograms, PMF & CDF

  • Histogram: Counts the raw frequency of observations falling into discrete bins.
  • Probability Mass Function (PMF): Normalized histogram where bin heights are divided by total samples n, representing discrete probabilities summing to 1.
  • Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF): Describes the probability that a real-valued random variable X will be less than or equal to x: F(x) = P(X ≤ x).

Outlier Detection & Treatment

# Domain-based outlier trimming on Adult dataset
# Filter reasonable working age between 22 and 72 years
df_cleaned = df.drop(df.index[
    (df['age'] > df['age'].median() + 35) | 
    (df['age'] < df['age'].median() - 15)
])
print("Mean age before:", df['age'].mean(), "After:", df_cleaned['age'].mean())

pages.title: Measuring Asymmetry & Continuous Distributions
pages.content_html:
2.4 Measuring Asymmetry & Continuous Distributions

Skewness & Pearson's Skewness Coefficient

Skewness characterizes the asymmetry of a distribution around its mean:

g1 = [1 / (n • σ³)] Σ (xi - μ)³

A symmetric or Gaussian distribution yields g1 = 0. Positive values indicate a longer right tail; negative values indicate a longer left tail.

Pearson's Median Skewness Coefficient:

gp = 3(μ - μ1/2) / σ

Common Continuous Distributions

Exponential Distribution

Models inter-arrival times between independent random events (e.g. radioactive decay, server requests):

CDF(x) = 1 - e-λx,   PDF(x) = λe-λx

Gaussian (Normal) Distribution

The ubiquitous bell-shaped curve describing natural and biological measurements:

PDF(x) = [1 / √(2πσ²)] • exp(-(x - μ)² / (2σ²))

Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)

When the true underlying distribution is unknown, non-parametric Kernel Density Estimation generates a smooth probability density curve by summing Gaussian kernels placed over every data point:

from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
density = gaussian_kde(sample_data)
x_grid = np.linspace(sample_data.min(), sample_data.max(), 200)
plt.plot(x_grid, density(x_grid), 'r-', linewidth=2)

pages.title: Estimation Theory, Confidence Intervals & Hypothesis Testing
pages.content_html:
2.5 Estimation Theory & Hypothesis Testing

Estimators & Standard Error (SE)

A point estimator approximates an unknown population parameter. By the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution with standard error:

SE = σ / √n

Confidence Intervals (CI)

A confidence interval establishes a plausible range of values: Θ ± z • SE.

  • 90% Confidence: z = 1.65
  • 95% Confidence: z = 1.96 &implies; CI = [x̄ - 1.96•SE, x̄ + 1.96•SE]
  • 99% Confidence: z = 2.58

Bootstrapping Simulation

# Bootstrapping 95% Confidence Interval for mean accident rate
def mean_bootstrap(data, iterations=10000):
    n = len(data)
    means = [np.mean(np.random.choice(data, size=n, replace=True)) for _ in range(iterations)]
    return np.percentile(means, 2.5), np.percentile(means, 97.5)

ci_low, ci_high = mean_bootstrap(accidents_data)
print(f"95% Bootstrapped CI: [{ci_low:.3f}, {ci_high:.3f}]")

Hypothesis Testing & p-Values

Null Hypothesis (H0): The observed difference is purely due to random chance.

Alternative Hypothesis (HA): The observed effect is real and statistically significant.

The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as our current sample assuming H0 is true. If p < 0.05, we reject H0 in favor of HA.

pages.title: Taxonomy of Machine Learning & Problem Formulation
pages.content_html:
3.1 Taxonomy of Machine Learning

Machine learning involves coding algorithms that automatically adapt their performance through exposure to training data. ML is broadly divided into three paradigms:

  1. Supervised Learning: Algorithms learn mapping functions from labeled input-output pairs (X → y) to predict outcomes on unseen test data (e.g. SVM, Decision Trees, Logistic Regression).
  2. Unsupervised Learning: Finding hidden geometric or statistical structures within unlabeled data (e.g. K-Means, PCA, Hierarchical Clustering).
  3. Reinforcement Learning: Agents learning optimal policy actions via environmental reward and penalty signals (e.g. Q-Learning, DRL).

Framing the Problem: Lending Club Case Study

We formulate a binary classification task on loan applications: predicting whether an approved loan will be fully funded (y = 1) or unfunded (y = -1). An application is defined as unsuccessful if the funded amount falls short by 5% or more of the requested amount:

(loan_amount - funded_amount) / loan_amount ≥ 0.05

The Scikit-Learn Object-Oriented Interface

  • Estimator.fit(X, y): Trains model parameters on the feature matrix X and target vector y.
  • Predictor.predict(X_new): Emits predicted categorical labels or continuous values.
  • Transformer.transform(X): Applies feature scaling, normalization, or encoding.

pages.title: K-Nearest Neighbors & The Accuracy Paradox
pages.content_html:
3.2 K-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN)

The k-NN classifier is a non-parametric instance-based algorithm. During training, it simply stores training samples in an n-dimensional metric space. To classify a new query point, it locates the k closest neighbors by Euclidean distance and takes a majority vote:

from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

# Train 11-NN classifier
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=11)
knn.fit(X_train, y_train)
accuracy = knn.score(X_test, y_test)
print(f"Classification Accuracy: {accuracy:.4f}")
# Output: 0.8316 (83.16%)

The Accuracy Paradox on Imbalanced Datasets

At first glance, 83.16% accuracy appears highly effective. However, examining the dataset label distribution reveals that 81.57% of loans are fully funded (positive class) and only 18.43% are unfunded (negative class).

A completely blind, trivial rule that simply predicts "fully funded" for every single loan achieves 81.57% accuracy with zero learned intelligence! Therefore, accuracy is an insufficient metric for imbalanced problems.

pages.title: Confusion Matrix & Advanced Metrics
pages.content_html:
3.3 Confusion Matrix & Evaluation Metrics

The Confusion Matrix provides a complete breakdown of actual versus predicted classes:

Actual PositiveActual NegativeRow Metric
Predicted PositiveTrue Positive (TP)False Positive (FP)Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
Predicted NegativeFalse Negative (FN)True Negative (TN)Negative Pred. Value = TN / (TN + FN)
Column MetricRecall (Sensitivity) = TP / (TP + FN)Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)Accuracy = (TP+TN) / Total

Key Metric Definitions

  • Sensitivity / Recall: Fraction of true positive cases correctly detected. Critical in medical diagnosis (cancer screening) and fraud detection where false negatives are dangerous.
  • Precision: Fraction of positive predictions that are truly positive. Critical in spam filters and criminal accusations where false alarms carry high penalties.
  • F1-Score: Harmonic mean of Precision and Recall:
    F1 = 2 • (Precision • Recall) / (Precision + Recall)
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report
y_pred = knn.predict(X_test)
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred))
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))

pages.title: Generalization, Overfitting & Learning Curves
pages.content_html:
3.4 Overfitting, Bias & Variance

Evaluating a model on the same data used for training produces In-Sample Error (Ein). A 1-NN model memorizes training instances perfectly (Ein = 0, 100% accuracy), but performs poorly on unseen data! The real performance metric is Out-of-Sample Generalization Error (Eout).

The Bias-Variance Decomposition

  • High Bias (Underfitting): The model is too simple (e.g. straight line for quadratic data). Both Ein and Eout are high.
  • High Variance (Overfitting): The model is overly complex (e.g. deep decision tree memorizing noise). Ein is low, but Eout explodes.

Cures for Overfitting

  1. Regularization: Penalizing complex weight vectors in the loss function:
    • L2 Ridge Regularization: Adds λ Σ wi², promoting smooth, small weights.
    • L1 LASSO Regularization: Adds λ Σ |wi|, driving irrelevant features to zero (sparsity).
  2. K-Fold Cross-Validation: Splitting data into K non-overlapping folds. Training on K-1 folds and evaluating on the held-out fold, repeated K times to obtain unbiased performance estimates.
  3. Ensemble Techniques: Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) and Boosting (combining multiple weak learners).

pages.title: Trees, SVM & Artificial Neural Networks
pages.content_html:
3.5 Core Supervised Algorithms

1. Decision Tree Classifiers (ID3)

Recursively partitions the feature space along axis-orthogonal hyperplanes to maximize Information Gain based on Shannon Entropy:

H(S) = - Σ pi log2(pi)

2. Support Vector Machines (SVM)

Finds the optimal separating hyperplane with Maximum Margin between classes:

min 0.5 • ||a||² + C Σ ξi   subject to yi(aTxi + b) ≥ 1 - ξi

Kernel Trick: Maps non-linear data into higher-dimensional feature spaces where linear separation is possible using the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel: k(xi, xj) = exp(-γ ||xi - xj||²).

3. Artificial Neural Networks & Backpropagation

Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) consist of input, hidden, and output neuron layers. The Backpropagation Algorithm computes error gradients using the calculus chain rule:

Δwij = η • δj • Oi

Weights are iteratively updated via gradient descent to minimize output loss.

pages.title: Linear Regression & Ordinary Least Squares
pages.content_html:
4.1 Linear Regression & Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)

Regression analysis models the relationship between a continuous response variable y and one or more independent predictor variables x. The simple linear regression model is:

y = a0 + a1x

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Estimator

OLS selects intercept a0 and slope a1 by minimizing the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE):

SSE = Σ (a0 + a1xj - yj)²

Case Study: Polar Sea Ice & Climate Change

Analyzing 36 years of National Snow & Ice Data Center monthly satellite records (1979-2014):

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# Normalize seasonal monthly fluctuations
for i in range(12):
    month_mask = (ice2['mo'] == i + 1)
    ice2.loc[month_mask, 'extent'] = 100 * (ice2.loc[month_mask, 'extent'] - month_means[i+1]) / month_means.mean()

# Fit OLS regression line
model = LinearRegression(fit_intercept=True)
model.fit(ice2[['year']], ice2['extent'])
print(f"Slope (rate of decline): {model.coef_[0]:.4f}% per year")
# Slope: -0.4528% per year (Proves significant long-term polar ice loss)

pages.title: Evaluating Regression, LASSO & Logistic Curves
pages.content_html:
4.2 Multiple Regression, LASSO & Logistic Models

Evaluating Regression Models

Mean Squared Error (MSE): MSE = (1 / n) Σ (yi - ŷi)²

Coefficient of Determination (R²):

R² = 1 - [Σ (yi - ŷi)² / Σ (yi - ȳ)²]

R² = 1.0 indicates perfect predictive performance; R² = 0 indicates performance no better than predicting the mean.

Sparse Modeling with LASSO

When datasets have many correlated or irrelevant features (e.g. Boston Housing dataset with 13 features), standard OLS suffers from high variance. LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) introduces an L1-norm penalty:

min [1 / (2n)] • ||Xw - y||² + α ||w||1

LASSO forces non-informative feature weights to exactly zero, performing automated feature selection!

Logistic Regression for Classification

When the target variable is binary (0 or 1), linear regression produces nonsensical predictions outside [0, 1]. Logistic Regression passes linear inputs through the Sigmoid function:

f(x) = 1 / (1 + e-λx)

pages.title: Unsupervised Learning & Distance Metrics
pages.content_html:
4.3 Unsupervised Clustering Foundations

Clustering partitions unlabeled data into disjoint clusters such that:

  • High Intraclass Similarity: Objects in the same cluster are very close.
  • Low Interclass Similarity: Objects in different clusters are far apart.

Distance & Similarity Metrics

The general Minkowski Distance between two vectors a, b is:

d(a, b) = (Σ |ai - bi|p)1/p
  • p = 2 &implies; Euclidean Distance: Straight-line geometric distance.
  • p = 1 &implies; Manhattan Distance: Grid-like city block distance.
  • p = ∞ &implies; Chebyshev Distance: Maximum component difference max |ai - bi|.

Evaluating Cluster Quality Without Ground Truth

  • Adjusted Rand Index (ARI): Measures clustering similarity adjusted for chance agreement (range: [-1, 1]).
  • V-Measure: Harmonic mean of Homogeneity and Completeness.
  • Silhouette Score: Measures how well-separated clusters are:
    s(i) = (b - a) / max(a, b)
    where a is intra-cluster distance and b is nearest-cluster distance. High values near +1 signify dense, well-isolated clusters.

pages.title: K-Means & K-Means++ Clustering
pages.content_html:
4.4 K-Means Clustering Algorithm

K-Means (Lloyd's Algorithm) partitions n samples into k clusters by minimizing within-cluster inertia:

Inertia = Σ Σ ||x - μj||²

Algorithmic Procedure

  1. Initialize: Select k initial centroids (randomly or via k-means++).
  2. Assign: Assign each data point to its closest centroid by Euclidean distance.
  3. Update: Recompute each centroid μj as the mean of all points assigned to it.
  4. Converge: Repeat steps 2 and 3 until cluster assignments stabilize.

The k-Means++ Advantage

Standard random initialization often converges to poor local minima. The k-means++ initialization scheme picks centroids that are probabilistically spread far apart from one another, drastically speeding up convergence and guaranteeing superior clustering solutions.

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# Fit K-Means on EU Education Expenditure indicators
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=4, init='k-means++', random_state=42)
cluster_labels = kmeans.fit_predict(edudrop)
print("Cluster Centroids:
", kmeans.cluster_centers_)

pages.title: Spectral & Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering
pages.content_html:
4.5 Spectral & Hierarchical Clustering

Spectral Clustering for Non-Convex Geometries

Standard K-Means assumes spherical, isotropic clusters and fails completely on concentric circles or interlocking moons. Spectral Clustering builds an affinity graph matrix A and solves the normalized graph Laplacian:

L = D-1/2 (D - A) D-1/2

Projecting points into the low-dimensional subspace of the smallest Laplacian eigenvectors separates complex, folded manifold structures effortlessly.

Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering

A bottom-up method that begins with each sample in its own cluster and iteratively joins the closest pair of clusters until one hierarchy remains. Visualized via Dendrograms.

Linkage CriterionMathematical DefinitionCluster Characteristics
Complete Linkagemax {d(x, y) : x ∈ A, y ∈ B}Compact, tight spherical clusters.
Average LinkageMean distance between all sample pairs in A and BBalanced; sensitive to noise/outliers.
Ward LinkageMinimizes increase in total within-cluster varianceMost regular, balanced, variance-minimizing clusters.

pages.title: Graph Theory Fundamentals & Network Topologies
pages.content_html:
5.1 Graph Theory & Network Topologies

Graph theory traces its origins to Leonhard Euler's resolution of the Seven Bridges of Königsberg (1735). A graph G = (V, E) consists of a set of nodes (vertices) V representing entities, and connecting edges (links) E representing relationships.

Graph Classifications

  • Undirected Graph: Symmetric relationship (e.g. mutual friendship, physical proximity).
  • Directed Graph (Digraph): Asymmetric arrows (e.g. Twitter follower, web hyperlinks).
  • Weighted Graph: Edges have quantitative values (e.g. highway distance, financial transfers).

Complex Network Models

  • Small-World Networks: Most nodes are not direct neighbors, but any node can be reached in very few steps (6 degrees of separation).
  • Scale-Free Networks: Node degree follows a power-law distribution P(k) ~ k-γ. Few massive hubs connect the entire system.

NetworkX in Python

import networkx as nx

# Loading Stanford SNAP Facebook Dataset (4,039 nodes, 88,234 edges)
fb = nx.read_edgelist('facebook_combined.txt')
print(f"Nodes: {fb.order()}, Edges: {fb.size()}")
print(f"Average Degree: {fb.size() / fb.order():.2f}")  # Avg degree = 21.8

pages.title: Graph Centrality Measures & PageRank
pages.content_html:
5.2 Centrality Measures & PageRank

Centrality measures the relative structural importance of nodes within a network graph:

MeasureMathematical ConceptNetwork Meaning
Degree CentralityCD(v) = deg(v) / (n - 1)Most connected popular nodes.
Betweenness CentralityRatio of shortest paths crossing node vGatekeeper nodes controlling information flow between communities.
Closeness CentralityInversely proportional to average distance to all nodesNodes that can rapidly communicate across the entire network.
Eigenvector CentralityProportional to sum of neighbor centralitiesNodes connected to other highly influential nodes.

The Google PageRank Algorithm

Invented by Larry Page & Sergey Brin (1998). Formulated as a Random Surfer Model with damping factor p = 0.85 to avoid dead ends:

R = (1 - p) M + p • (1 / n) I

The transition probability vector converges iteratively (vk+1 = M vk) to a unique stationary eigenvector a*.

pages.title: Ego-Networks & Community Detection
pages.content_html:
5.3 Ego-Networks & Community Detection

Ego-Networks

An ego-network consists of a focal node (the ego) and all its direct neighbors (the alters), along with all links connecting those alters.

  • Radius 1 Ego-Network: Direct friends of node '107' (1,046 nodes).
  • Radius 2 Ego-Network: Friends-of-friends of node '107' (2,687 nodes — over 66% of the whole Facebook graph!).
# Extracting ego-network using NetworkX
ego_107 = nx.ego_graph(fb, '107', radius=1)
print(f"Ego 107 Node Count: {len(ego_107)}")

Community Detection: The Louvain Method

A community is a cluster of graph nodes with high internal edge density and sparse external connections. The Louvain Method optimizes graph modularity Q through a greedy hierarchical algorithm:

import community as community_louvain

# Extract communities from Facebook graph
partition = community_louvain.best_partition(fb)
num_communities = len(set(partition.values()))
print(f"Extracted {num_communities} distinct social communities!")

pages.title: Generative Deep Learning & Transformer Models
pages.content_html:
5.4 Generative AI & Transformers

Generative Deep Learning Paradigms

  • Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs): A minimax zero-sum game between Generator G and Discriminator D:
    min_G max_D V(D, G) = E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))]
  • Variational Autoencoders (VAEs): Maps inputs to probabilistic latent vectors optimizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO):
    L = E[log P(X|z)] - D_KL(Q(z|X) || P(z))
  • Diffusion Models: Adds progressive Gaussian noise across forward steps and trains a neural network to iteratively denoise the latent field.

Transformer Architectures & Self-Attention

Eliminating sequential RNN recurrence by processing entire token sequences concurrently via Scaled Dot-Product Attention:

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax((Q • KT) / √dk) • V
  • Encoder Models (BERT): Bidirectional attention for classification & NER.
  • Decoder Models (GPT): Causal autoregressive masking for generative text completion.

pages.title: Distributed Big Data Systems & Apache Spark
pages.content_html:
5.5 Distributed Big Data: Apache Spark

When dataset volumes exceed single-machine RAM, distributed cluster computing frameworks partition and execute workloads in parallel.

Apache Spark Architecture

Governed by a central Driver Program interacting with a Cluster Manager (YARN, Kubernetes) to dispatch execution tasks across Worker Node Executors.

Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs)

  • Immutable: Datasets cannot be mutated; operations produce new RDD pointers.
  • Partitioned: Data splits physically across cluster nodes.
  • Fault-Tolerant via Lineage: RDDs record the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of transformations, allowing instant recreation if a node fails.

Lazy Evaluation vs Eager Actions

Transformations (.map(), .filter()) are evaluated lazily by appending operational nodes to the DAG. Execution is triggered only when an Action (.count(), .collect()) is invoked.

Advanced Spark Ecosystem

  • Spark SQL & Catalyst Optimizer: Optimizes queries via predicate pushdown, rule-based heuristics, and runtime Janino Java bytecode generation.
  • Columnar Parquet: High-speed columnar storage reading only queried columns.
  • Structured Streaming: Real-time event ingestion over unbounded tables with watermarking.
  • GraphX: Distributed graph processing with VertexRDD and EdgeRDD abstractions.
  • Spark MLlib: Scalable machine learning pipelines with CrossValidator tuning.
